title: Phil 101 — Reading Options (Days 4–27)
text:
A menu to sort, not a final list. Bias throughout: short, structured, freely available, friendly to non-majors. Each line is: citation — link — free? · length · why it fits. Days 6–9 are already chosen and marked accordingly. Long primary texts (Mill, Kant, Foot, Thomson, Crito, On Liberty) are flagged “excerpt”; the Early Modern Texts editions are genuinely free, public-domain, and modernized for readability.





Required: Jonathan Weisberg, “The Grue Paradox” (Odds & Ends, open textbook, ch. C) — https://jonathanweisberg.org/vip/grue.html — free; ~2,000 words, self-contained, with a built-in grue-and-AI section.
Recommended: Sven Neth, “Goodman’s New Riddle of Induction Explained in Words of One Syllable” — https://philpapers.org/archive/NETGNR.pdf — free; ~1,000 words.
Recommended: Nelson Goodman, Fact, Fiction, and Forecast, ch. 3 “The New Riddle of Induction” — http://fitelson.org/confirmation/goodman_1955.pdf — the comprehensive source (linked, not hosted; a lot for a first reading).








Required: Todd R. Long, “Epistemic Justification: What is Rational Belief?” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2023/03/19/epistemic-justification/ — free; 999 words.
Required: IEP, “Foundationalism,” §§1–2 (“Knowledge and Justification”; “Arguments for Foundationalism”) — https://iep.utm.edu/foundationalism-in-epistemology/ — free. In lecture, flag that we want the version taking perceptions as the foundation (that variety is in §4); IEP rather than SEP, which goes into the weeds too fast.
Required: SEP, “Epistemology in Classical Indian Philosophy,” §1.1 “Knowledge and Knowledge Sources” — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epistemology-india/ — free; ~1,200–1,500 words. The pramāṇa framing; the how-many-sources ladder (§§6–7) carried in lecture.
Recommended: James Pryor, “Highlights of Recent Epistemology” (BJPS 2001) — https://www.jimpryor.net/research/papers/Highlights.pdf — free PDF; for the very keen — surveys modest foundationalism (including his perception view), contextualism, and the internalism/externalism debate.





Required: SEP, “Epistemological Problems of Memory,” §2.4 (Preservationism and Generativism) — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/memory-episprob/
Recommended: Lisa K. Fazio et al., “Knowledge Does Not Protect Against Illusory Truth” — https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/features/xge-0000098.pdf





Dhirendra Mohan Datta, “Testimony as a Method of Knowledge,” Mind 36 (1927): 354–358.
Optional: Sperber et al., “Epistemic Vigilance,” Mind & Language 25 (2010).





Required: Elizabeth Anderson, “Democracy, Public Policy, and Lay Assessments of Scientific Testimony,” Episteme (2011), §2 only, “Principles for Second-Order Lay Assessment of Scientific Claims” (pp. 145–149) — the three trustworthiness criteria (expertise, honesty, epistemic responsibility), how to judge a consensus, and the dialogic-irrationality example. (Tighter still: pp. 145–147 carry the three criteria.)
Recommended: the full Anderson paper — beyond §2 it sets up the democratic-legitimacy problem (§1), works the climate case study (§3), and diagnoses why Americans distrust experts (§§4–5).
Recommended: SEP, “The Social Dimensions of Scientific Knowledge,” §2 “Big Science, Trust, and Authority” — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-knowledge-social/ — ~3,000 words · epistemic dependence in science (Hardwig): big teams trust results no one person fully checks, with live cases (cold fusion, Wakefield/MMR). Replaces the Case piece, whose Reid-vs-Hume framing clashed with the Nyāya story from Day 7.





Required: C. Thi Nguyen, “Escape the Echo Chamber” (Aeon) — https://aeon.co/essays/why-its-as-hard-to-escape-an-echo-chamber-as-it-is-to-flee-a-cult — free; ~4,600 words, enough on its own (epistemic bubbles vs echo chambers).
Recommended: Naomi Oreskes interview, “Defending science in a post-fact era” (Harvard Gazette, 2019) — https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2019/10/in-why-trust-science-naomi-oreskes-explains-why-the-process-of-proof-is-worth-trusting/ — free; a long-read Q&A laying out her five pillars of trustworthy science (consensus, diversity, method, evidence, values), the “why trust science” half. Meatier than the short Princeton blurb, now dropped.
Recommended (rigorous version): C. Thi Nguyen, “Echo Chambers and Epistemic Bubbles,” Episteme 17 (2020): 141–161 — gated; for the keen. By Nguyen’s own note the Aeon piece is the general-audience rendering of this paper; the journal version adds the precise definitions, the bootstrapped-corroboration argument, and a Hardwig dependence cite that ties back to Day 8.








Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy, ch. 1 “Appearance and Reality” — https://www.gutenberg.org/files/5827/5827-h/5827-h.htm — free · ~2,000 words · the classic table example; ideal short primary anchor.
SEP, “The Problem of Perception,” §2 “The Argument from Illusion” — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/perception-problem/ — free · assign one section (~2,000 words) · illusion/hallucination and the sense-datum vs naive-realist responses.
IEP, “Sense-Data” (Huemer) — https://iep.utm.edu/sense-da/ — free · moderate · more readable sense-data intro if SEP feels dense.
Note: no dedicated 1000-Word essay on the problem of perception; Russell is the short anchor.





Thomas Nagel, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” (1974) — https://rintintin.colorado.edu/~vancecd/phil201/Nagel.pdf — free (course PDF) · ~16 pp · the canonical anchor for qualia and subjectivity, vivid and non-technical.
Jacob Berger, “The Mind-Body Problem: What Are Minds?” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2024/02/03/mind-body-problem/ — free · 998 words · tight primer that ends on Nagel’s bat.
Keith Frankish, “The Consciousness Illusion” (Aeon) — https://aeon.co/essays/what-if-your-consciousness-is-an-illusion-created-by-your-brain — free · ~4,000 words · provocative discussion-sparker.





Tufan Kıymaz, “The Knowledge Argument Against Physicalism” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2019/10/05/the-knowledge-argument-against-physicalism/ — free · ~1,000 words · clean anchor laying out Mary and the standard replies.
Frank Jackson, “What Mary Didn’t Know” (1986) — https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys419/sp2021/Jackson1986_WhatMaryDidntKnow.pdf — free (course PDF) · ~5 pp · short primary (longer “Epiphenomenal Qualia” 1982, ~10 pp, also free).
David Chalmers, “Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness” (1995) — https://consc.net/papers/facing.pdf — free · long (assign the easy-vs-hard opening) · origin of the “hard problem.”





Jacob Berger, “The Mind-Body Problem” (1000-Word Philosophy), “Varieties of Dualism” section — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2024/02/03/mind-body-problem/ — free · 998 words · compact statement of dualism and the conceivability argument.
René Descartes, Meditations II and VI (Bennett, Early Modern Texts) — https://www.earlymoderntexts.com/assets/pdfs/descartes1641.pdf — free · II ~5 pp, VI ~7 pp · the cogito and the real distinction, in plain modernized English.
Peter Adamson, “What can Avicenna teach us about the mind-body problem?” (Aeon Ideas) — https://aeon.co/ideas/what-can-avicenna-teach-us-about-the-mind-body-problem — free · short · the flying man (denser alternative: SEP “Ibn Sina,” psychology section).





Jacob Berger, “The Mind-Body Problem” (1000-Word Philosophy), identity-theory / functionalism + interaction objection — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2024/02/03/mind-body-problem/ — free · 998 words · the physicalism half of the same essay.
Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia – Descartes correspondence (1643) (Bennett, Early Modern Texts) — https://www.earlymoderntexts.com/assets/pdfs/descelis.pdf — free · a few pages · the interaction objection in her own words.
IEP, “Identity Theory” (Schneider) — https://iep.utm.edu/identity/ — free · moderate (assign intro) · physicalism intro (functionalism: IEP “Functionalism,” https://iep.utm.edu/functism/).








Shane Gronholz, “Consequentialism and Utilitarianism” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2014/05/15/consequentialism/ — free · ~1,000 words · plain anchor, act vs rule without jargon.
J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.net) — https://utilitarianism.net/books/utilitarianism-john-stuart-mill/2/ — free · long (excerpt the greatest-happiness and higher/lower-pleasures passages) · the canonical statement.
Brandon Boesch, “Ethics and Absolute Poverty: Singer and Effective Altruism” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2021/03/05/ethics-and-absolute-poverty/ — free · ~1,000 words · vivid application (the drowning child).





Andrew Chapman, “Deontology: Kantian Ethics” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2014/06/09/introduction-to-deontology-kantian-ethics/ — free · ~999 words · anchor; both formulations of the Categorical Imperative in everyday terms.
Kant, Groundwork, Section I (Bennett, Early Modern Texts) — https://www.earlymoderntexts.com/assets/pdfs/kant1785.pdf — free · ~5,000 words (excerpt the good-will opening and universal-law passages) · primary, modernized.
SEP, “Deontological Ethics,” §1 “Deontology’s Foil: Consequentialism” — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-deontological/ — free · short section · a crisp definition by contrast.





Gabriel Andrade, “The Doctrine of Double Effect” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2023/03/11/doctrine-of-double-effect/ — free · ~1,000 words · anchor; switch vs footbridge and the foresee/intend distinction.
Philippa Foot, “The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect” (1967) — https://philpapers.org/archive/footpo-2.pdf — free · ~11 pp (excerpt the opening) · where the trolley case was born.
Judith Jarvis Thomson, “The Trolley Problem” (1985) — https://openyls.law.yale.edu/handle/20.500.13051/16338 — free (Yale) · ~21 pp (excerpt) · the footbridge contrast (lighter, critical contrast: Aeon, “What is the problem with ethical trolley problems?”).








SEP, “Well-Being,” §1 “The Concept of Well-Being” (Crisp) — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/well-being/ — free · ~1,500 words · motivates fixing welfare by its role; the methodological anchor.
“Theories of Well-Being” (utilitarianism.net), intro — https://utilitarianism.net/theories-of-wellbeing/ — free · ~5 min · plainest map of the three theories.
Note: no free 101-length Keller piece confirmed; use Keller as instructor background.





SEP, “Well-Being,” §4.1 “Hedonism” — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/well-being/ — free · ~700–900 words · tight statement plus objections.
Robert Nozick, “The Experience Machine” (excerpt) — https://rintintin.colorado.edu/~vancecd/phil3160/Nozick1.pdf — free (course PDF) · ~2 pp · the vivid anti-hedonism test case.
“Happiness: What Is It to Be Happy?” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2021/05/08/happiness/ — free · ~1,000 words · closest 1000-Word piece (no standalone hedonism essay).





SEP, “Well-Being,” §4.2 “Desire Theories” — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/well-being/ — free · ~900 words · the theory plus the standard objections.
“Theories of Well-Being,” desire-theory section (utilitarianism.net) — https://utilitarianism.net/theories-of-wellbeing/#desire-theories — free · ~700 words · more example-driven alternative.
Remote/posthumous-desire illustration: in SEP §4.2, or the course handout “What Is a Good Life?” — https://rintintin.colorado.edu/~vancecd/phil1100/Well.pdf





SEP, “Well-Being,” §4.3 “Objective List Theories” — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/well-being/ — free · ~700 words · compact intro and the alienation objection.
“The Moral Status of Animals” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2014/02/03/the-moral-status-of-animals/ — free · ~1,000 words · sentience and moral standing (pair with “Speciesism,” https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2014/03/20/speciesism/).
“If AIs Can Feel Pain, What Is Our Responsibility Towards Them?” (Aeon, on Sebo’s work) — https://aeon.co/essays/if-ais-can-feel-pain-what-is-our-responsibility-towards-them — free · ~3,000 words · accessible AI-welfare entry (primary: Sebo & Long, “Moral Consideration for AI Systems by 2030,” https://jeffsebo.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/moral-consideration-for-ai-systems-by-2030-5.pdf).








Kristin Seemuth Whaley, “Psychological Approaches to Personal Identity” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2022/02/03/psychological-approaches-to-personal-identity/ — free · ~1,000 words · anchor; walks the teleporter/fission puzzles.
Chad Vance, “Personal Identity: How We Exist Over Time” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2014/02/10/personal-identity/ — free · ~1,000 words · the general persistence framing.
Derek Parfit, “Divided Minds and the Nature of Persons” (1987) — https://rintintin.colorado.edu/~vancecd/phil375/Parfit.pdf — free (course PDF, in copyright) · ~5–6 pp · Parfit’s own accessible teletransporter/fission (reference: SEP “Personal Identity,” §4 or §5).





John Locke, Essay II.xxvii “Of Identity and Diversity,” §§9–26 (Bennett, Early Modern Texts) — https://www.earlymoderntexts.com/assets/pdfs/locke1690book2_4.pdf — free · the prince-and-cobbler passage; the forensic-person anchor.
Daniel Weltman, “The Buddhist Theory of No-Self (Anātman/Anattā)” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2023/02/25/no-self/ — free · ~1,000 words · clear intro to anattā, pairs with Parfit’s reductionism.
Derek Parfit, “Divided Minds and the Nature of Persons” (reused from Day 22) — reductionism and “what matters.”








Plato, Crito (Jowett trans., Project Gutenberg #1657) — https://www.gutenberg.org/files/1657/1657-h/1657-h.htm — free · ~15–20 pp, fast dialogue · the obvious anchor.
Spencer Case, “Plato’s Crito: When Should We Break the Law?” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2018/12/30/platos-crito-when-should-we-break-the-law/ — free · ~1,000 words · structured scaffolding for the dialogue.
SEP, “Political Obligation” (Dagger & Lefkowitz), intro section — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/political-obligation/ — free · assign the intro · modern framing of “why obey the law.”





Travis Joseph Rodgers, “Theories of Punishment” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2019/02/05/theories-of-punishment/ — free · ~995 words · anchor; forward-looking vs backward-looking in clean sections.
SEP, “Legal Punishment” (Duff & Hoskins), consequentialist + retributivist sections — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/legal-punishment/ — free · assign the two named sections · the desert-vs-deterrence debate.
Optional primary: J.S. Mill, “Speech in Favour of Capital Punishment” (1868) — confirm a clean host before assigning.





J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 “Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion” (Project Gutenberg #34901) — https://www.gutenberg.org/files/34901/34901-h/34901-h.htm — free · long (excerpt to the “four distinct grounds”) · the canonical anchor.
Mark Satta, “Free Speech” (1000-Word Philosophy) — https://1000wordphilosophy.com/2021/02/04/free-speech/ — free · ~1,000 words · clean pre-class framing (the author works in philosophy and law).





David V. Johnson, “How do we pry apart the true and compelling from the false and toxic?” (Aeon Ideas, 2019) — https://aeon.co/ideas/how-do-we-pry-apart-the-true-and-compelling-from-the-false-and-toxic — free · ~1,100 words · directly tests Mill’s optimism against troll farms and cognitive bubbles.
C. Thi Nguyen, “Escape the Echo Chamber” (Aeon) — https://aeon.co/essays/why-its-as-hard-to-escape-an-echo-chamber-as-it-is-to-flee-a-cult — free · long (excerpt) · the core epistemic critique (already on the Day 9 menu; could extend rather than repeat).






Course-hosted PDFs (Nagel, Jackson, Chalmers, Nozick excerpt, Parfit) are widely-used teaching copies of in-copyright work; they resolve now but verify before term, and Parfit especially is not formally free.
Long primary texts (Mill’s Utilitarianism ch. 2 and On Liberty ch. 2, Kant’s Groundwork I, Foot, Thomson, Crito) need named excerpts to stay within a non-major’s tolerance.
Several gaps in 1000-Word Philosophy: no live essay on the problem of induction, the problem of perception, welfare/well-being, or hedonism. The SEP “Well-Being” entry assigned section by section (§1, §4.1, §4.2, §4.3) is the single best reusable spine for Days 18–21.

The load-bearing connections, so they survive edits:

The first four classes are reasoning and inference; 5 to 9 are the epistemology of evidence and testimony. Perceptual evidentialism (5–6) now comes before testimony (7–9), so testimony has something to be measured against. Memory (6) is the bridge: a forgotten-source belief is usually forgotten testimony.
Hume on miracles lives inside the testimony class at 7, as the lead reductionist case Datta answers, rather than in a religion unit.
The mind unit opens by reconsidering perception (10). We leaned on perception as evidence for the whole epistemology unit; now we crack the bedrock open. The flying man opens the unit as a hook and pays off at 13.
The self unit ends on Locke’s forensic person (23), which hands to law and politics: the person is whoever can be held responsible.
Law and politics runs authority, then coercion, then limits: Crito on why to obey, punishment on what the state may do to you, free speech on what it may not. Free speech at 27 closes the loop back to the first half, testing the marketplace of ideas against echo chambers, the illusory truth effect, and manufactured controversy.

Calendar fit: the Fall break still lands exactly at the mind-to-ethics seam. Thanksgiving now falls at a clean join, after Crito and before punishment, with Crito as a self-contained dialogue that suits a thin pre-holiday Tuesday and the punishment-and-free-speech stretch running unbroken after.
Deliberately left out: philosophy of religion (replaced by law and politics, with miracles kept and moved into the testimony class), free will, and the meaning-of-life topics. The buffer is a single slack day at 28; expect units to grow.
Slide files still to renumber to match this order (05 becomes Evidence I, the memory deck becomes 06, the Datta deck becomes 07, Anderson 08, Oreskes and Nguyen 09).
Parked in planning, not yet placed: the 2026 “old debates, new instances” asides (kept varied across technologies, not all LLMs), and two take-home discussion questions, belief versus representation (end of mind) and the identity conditions of an AI (end of personal identity).

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
Testimony turned out to be a source in its own right, though a guarded one. You trust by default, and you keep a quiet watch on the source and the content.
. . .
That watch works while you can size a person up. It runs out fast.



Almost nothing you believe about the world came from someone you could vet. The size of an atom, the age of the universe, the safety of a drug: you hold it on the word of experts you will never meet.
So the real question is not whether to trust testimony. It is how to judge the people you have no choice but to depend on.

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
You cannot redo the work
To check the climate science yourself you would need years of training you do not have. The same goes for the vaccine, the bridge, the diagnosis.
This is not a personal failing. No one has the hours to become expert in everything, so all of us lean on others for nearly all of what we know.

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
Testimony all the way in
John Hardwig pointed out that even scientists are in this spot. A big experiment runs on a team where no one member understands all the evidence, so each takes the others’ results on trust.
So you are back to trust, only now the speaker is a stranger with a doctorate whom even her colleagues cannot fully check.

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
The bind
You cannot assess the science. You still have to decide what to believe, and sometimes what to do about it.
If you cannot judge the work, what can you judge?

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
A Michigan answer
Elizabeth Anderson, who teaches philosophy here, has the cleanest reply. You stop trying to grade the research, and you assess the researchers instead.
That is a second-order judgment, about people and institutions rather than about the science itself, and it is one you are equipped to make.

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
What to look for
Anderson points to three things an ordinary person can check with no more than schooling and a search engine:

expertise: are they trained and credentialed in the field they are speaking on?
honesty: is there a record of fraud, hidden funding, or past deception?
responsibility: do they answer their critics and put their work up for scrutiny?

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
The point of the list
None of this asks you to follow the science. It asks you to read a record, trace who paid for what, and see whether someone hides from challenge or invites it.
The judgment shifts from the claim to the claimant, where a layperson can actually stand.

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
You are doing it now
This is your own position in this room. You are taking a course largely on my say-so.
. . .
So run Anderson’s checks on me, and on her. Her office is a short walk from this one. The criteria point straight back at the people teaching them to you.

title: Whom Do You Trust?
text:
A harder case
The checks work best when the trustworthy experts agree. When credentialed, honest, careful people land on opposite sides, second-order judgment gets harder.
That is where we go next: what a consensus is worth, and how one can be faked.

Reading
Required:

Elizabeth Anderson, “Democracy, Public Policy, and Lay Assessments of Scientific Testimony,” Episteme (2011), §2 (pp. 145–149).

Recommended: the rest of that paper, and SEP, “The Social Dimensions of Scientific Knowledge,” §2 (“Big Science, Trust, and Authority”).

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
We set perception and inference on one side and asked where testimony goes. Is it a third source, or does it fold into the other two?
. . .
Today we take the reducing view seriously, lean on it, and see what is left standing.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
section: It is just perception and inference
text:
It is just perception and inference
The reductionist says testimony is not basic. Someone tells you the bridge is out. You hear the words, which is perception, and you conclude they are true, which is inference, because people of that sort, on roads of that sort, have been right before.
Your belief rests on perception and an inference from the speaker’s reliability. Testimony adds no new way of knowing.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
Why hold it
The view is tidy. It keeps the list of sources short, and it makes trust earn its place. You believe a speaker because you have evidence that speakers like this are reliable, and not otherwise.
Hume reasons this way about reports of miracles, setting the testimony against everything the rest of experience tells us.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
The plan
Two objections do most of the damage. The first says the reductionist can never get started. The second says the standard it sets is too harsh, and would sink perception along with testimony.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
We do not actually infer
Watch yourself take in what people say. You believe it straight off, unless something trips an alarm. You do not stop to build an argument from the speaker’s track record.
Datta quotes Montague on the point:

Man is a suggestible animal and tends to believe what is said to him unless he has some positive reason for doubting the honesty or competence of his informant.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
The well runs dry
Suppose belief did wait on an inference from past reliability. Where would the evidence come from?
You would need a stock of cases checked for yourself, with no one’s word taken. But almost everything you know about speakers, roads, and bridges arrived by testimony in the first place. The inference has nothing of its own to stand on.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
Two questions, kept apart
Datta’s key move is to pull apart two things the reductionist runs together:

where the content of a belief comes from
how its truth gets checked

Testimony can be the source of the content even when the checking is done by some other route.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
In his words

The attempt to reduce testimony to inference is based on a confusion between the source of a knowledge and the source of the knowledge of its validity.

You learn from a friend that he is glad. His words are the source of that fact. An inference might confirm that he is truthful, but it says nothing about his being glad. That came from him.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
Turn it on perception
The reductionist demands that real knowledge be checkable by some other method. Datta turns the demand around.

If testimony ceases to be a source of knowledge because the truth of it has to be ascertained through inference, why should not even perception cease to be a source of knowledge?

Perceptions mislead too, and we check them against further perceptions. By the reductionist’s own rule, perception would reduce as well. The rule proves too much.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
Anti-reductionism
Put the two criticisms together. We trust without inferring, and the demand that would disqualify testimony would disqualify the rest. So testimony looks like a source in its own right, level with perception and inference.
This is the Nyāya view Datta defends, and roughly the one much later writers worked their way back to.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
The gullibility worry
If we trust by default, we look like easy marks. A great deal of testimony is mistaken, and some of it is built to fool us. A theory that has us swallowing whatever we are told cannot be right either.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
Trust, but filtered
Sperber, Mercier, and their colleagues in Paris offer a way through. We are neither blank trusters nor blanket doubters. We run a set of quiet checks as we listen:

on the source: is this person competent, and do they mean me well?
on the content: does this sit with what I already have good reason to believe?

Default trust is where we start, but it passes through a filter.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
What the filter buys
This keeps both halves of the picture. We can learn from each other, which is the whole point of testimony, without lying at the mercy of every liar.
The trust is real, and so is the guard. That is how testimony can be basic without making us fools.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
section: A job we cannot yet hand off
text:
A job we cannot yet hand off
Vigilance is so ordinary that we hardly notice doing it. Building it is another matter.
A system that takes in testimony at scale, trained on whatever it is fed, has no steady grip on whether a source can be trusted or whether a claim hangs together. The check a child runs without trying is something we do not know how to engineer.
. . .
It is the shape from the grue week once more. The hard part was never the storing. It is the prior judgment about what to trust.

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
For next time

Dhirendra Mohan Datta, “Testimony as a Method of Knowledge,” Mind 36 (1927): 354–358.

Five pages, and decades ahead of its field.
If you want the vigilance idea first-hand: Sperber et al., “Epistemic Vigilance,” Mind & Language 25 (2010).

title: Does Testimony Stand on Its Own?
text:
Where we land
Testimony stands on its own feet, but vigilant feet. You trust, and you watch.
Next we follow that out: whom to trust when you cannot check, and how to weigh experts who disagree.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
In the deduction game, a verdict was allowed only when the clues forced it. The conclusion was already sitting inside what you were given.
. . .
That safety has a price. A valid deduction never hands you anything that wasn’t, in some form, already in the premises.



To learn something new about the world, you have to take a risk. You have to draw a conclusion that runs past your evidence, and so might be wrong.
Inferences of that kind are the subject of today.



We will look at three ways of reasoning past the evidence:

enumerative induction
argument from analogy
inference to the best explanation

By the end there is a case that the first two are versions of the third.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
From some to all
You observe a run of cases and project the pattern onto the ones you have not seen.
Every raven anyone has recorded has been black, so the next raven will be black, and perhaps all of them are.
. . .
The premises can be true and the conclusion false. The inference is risky by design.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
The leap is the point
Nothing in the black ravens you have seen forces a colour on the raven you have not. The move from seen to unseen is a leap.
We make it all the time, and mostly it pays. Why it pays is a question we press tomorrow.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
From like to like
Two things are alike in several respects, so they are probably alike in one more.
A new drug cured the disease in mice. Mice and humans share the relevant biology, so the drug may cure it in humans.
. . .
The whole weight of the inference rests on whether the similarities are the ones that matter.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
From clues to cause
You have some facts to account for. You ask which hypothesis, if it were true, would best explain them, and you conclude that it is true.
This is the detective’s move, so let us bring in the detective.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
Holmes at the pool
In “The Boscombe Valley Mystery,” Holmes reaches the scene and changes:

Sherlock Holmes was transformed when he was hot upon such a scent as this… His nostrils seemed to dilate with a purely animal lust for the chase.

He crawls over the ground with a lens, reading the trampled grass.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
What he calls it
Holmes calls his method deduction. It is no such thing.
From the stride, the boots, and a scrap of cigar ash, he settles on a tall, left-handed man who smokes Indian cigars. None of that is forced. It is the account that fits the marks better than any rival, and that is why he backs it.
. . .
That is inference to the best explanation, wearing a famous disguise.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
Two jobs, not one
Watch Holmes work in two stages.
At the pool he gathers: the lens, the ash, the prints in the grass. That is perception.
Back at the inn he expounds, fitting the clues into one story. That is inference.
. . .
Holmes names the pair himself: “a trivial example of observation and inference. Therein lies my métier.”

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
section: Why the best, and not merely one
text:
Why the best, and not merely one
Holmes warns Watson off the easy reading:

There is nothing more deceptive than an obvious fact.

The work is not finding an explanation. It is finding the one that beats its rivals. He sets himself a rule for the case, to treat the son’s story as true and follow where that leads.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
One move underneath
Harman’s suggestion is that the other two are inference to the best explanation in plainer clothes.
Take the ravens. Calling “all ravens are black” the best explanation of the run you have seen is what licenses the jump to the next one. The mice work the same way, with shared biology as the best explanation of the shared cure.
. . .
You need not accept this to use it. It is a way of seeing what the three have in common.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
What they share
Each one reaches past the evidence to something the evidence does not force. That reach is what makes them useful, and what makes them fallible.
Holmes’s whole art lives in that gap, between the marks on the ground and the man who left them.

title: Risky Inferences: Induction, Analogy, Explanation
text:
Where this leaves us
Every inference today began from something given: ravens already seen, results already in, marks already on the ground.
Tomorrow we ask what happens when even a spotless run of evidence fails to pin the answer down. That is the grue problem.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
Grue left us with a problem. A run of evidence, however clean, does not on its own fix what comes next. Inference needs something fed in from outside.
So the question for today is a plain one: what feeds it?



In the deduction game the clues were handed to you, and they were true. That is the only reason you never had to guess.
. . .
Nothing outside the game works like that. No one hands you clues that are both given and guaranteed. So where do real clues come from?



We watched Holmes observe and infer. Look again at where his information actually comes from:

a telegram summons him to the case
the newspaper prints the inquest, and he reads the son’s statement on the train
Miss Turner comes to the inn and tells him about her father
Lestrade passes on what the police have found

. . .
His own eyes meet the evidence for the first time only at the pool. The rest he is working from because someone told him.



Believing something because someone told you has a name. It is testimony.
It sits awkwardly beside the other two. You did not see it for yourself, and you did not work it out. You took someone’s word.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
How many sources are there?
Long before Hume, philosophers in India asked just this and gave it a name. A pramāṇa is a source of knowledge, a way a true belief can be properly arrived at. The argument was over how many there are.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
The ladder

the Cārvāka materialists allow one: perception
the Buddhist logicians allow two: perception and inference
the Nyāya school allows four: perception, inference, comparison, and testimony
later schools press on, reaching six

. . .
The four-source list adds two things the two-source list lacks: comparison, and the one that will occupy us, testimony.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
A word on comparison
Comparison is the unfamiliar one. The stock example: you are told that a wild ox is much like a cow, you later meet the animal in the forest, and you know at once which kind it is.
That is the analogy from Day 3 put to a narrow job, fixing what a new word picks out by its likeness to something you already know.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
section: The model you have been using
text:
The model you have been using
Our own tradition mostly settled on the two: perception and inference. You have spent the week living inside that picture.
The game was inference. Holmes was perception feeding inference. Neither left room for testimony as a source in its own right.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
The question
Set perception and inference on one side. Does testimony belong beside them as a third source, or does it fold into them, so that you perceive the words and then infer that they are true?
We take that up in full next class. First, why it is worth the trouble.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
Why it matters
Strip testimony out and look at what survives in what you know.
Nearly all of history, the sciences, and geography reached you on someone’s word, and so did most of what you treat as your own memory of early childhood. If testimony is not a way of knowing, most of your knowledge is not knowledge after all.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
section: An old argument, an unlikely place
text:
An old argument, an unlikely place
The dispute is not new. In 1927 an Indian philosopher, Dhirendra Mohan Datta, argued the case in Mind, putting the Nyāya side to his Cambridge contemporaries.
We read him next class. Today, get the lay of the land.

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
Reading
For the map of the Indian debate, its schools, its sources, and the arguments between them:

“Epistemology in Classical Indian Philosophy,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. plato.stanford.edu/entries/epistemology-india

title: How Many Sources of Knowledge?
text:
Where this goes
Next class, the question head on. Does testimony stand on its own feet? The reductionist says no, and we will see how hard that is to make stick.
. . .
Further out sit the questions it opens. Whom to trust when you cannot check for yourself. How to weigh experts who disagree. Why we lean on science. And the hardest report of all, that a miracle occurred.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
We set up the evidentialist picture. Your beliefs answer to your evidence, and perception is the clearest case of first-hand evidence, the kind you check for yourself.
. . .
But perception is gone in a moment. What you actually carry around, and act on, is the residue: what you remember.



A fact about memory, from the lab and from a second’s introspection alike: it stores contents, not sources.
You remember that the heart has four chambers. You do not remember where you learned it, from whom, or whether the source was any good.
. . .
It keeps even less than the content, but set that aside for today.



The result is a head full of beliefs whose origins you have lost. You know a great many things and could not say, for almost any of them, how you came to know them.
Most of the time that is fine. Sometimes it is the whole problem.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
A case you will recognize
Years ago you picked some claim up from a poor source: a half-read headline, a confident friend who turned out to be wrong, a guess you made under pressure.
You long ago forgot where it came from. Now you simply believe it, and it feels like something you know.
. . .
This is not a thought experiment. It is most of what sits in anyone’s head.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
The puzzle
Put it as cleanly as we can. Almost all of your belief-forming methods are reliable; one of them is not. You formed the belief that p by the unreliable one, and then forgot that you had.
Today you have a memory that p, and nothing else.
Are you justified in believing p?

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
It pulls two ways
No. The belief came from a bad method and never picked up any new support along the way. Bad in, bad out.
Yes. Your memories are mostly of reliable things, so any given remembered belief is a fair bet, and the bad origin is gone. Forgetting laundered it.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
The fork, without the jargon
The two answers grade the belief by different things. One looks back at where it came from. The other looks at how trustworthy your memory is in general.
Both have a real pull, and that is the puzzle. You do not need a theory of justification to feel it.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
section: It is how being wrong sticks
text:
It is how being wrong sticks
This is no curiosity. It is the mechanism behind a good deal of what we get wrong.
You meet a shaky claim, you discount it, you forget the source, you keep the claim. Months later it has shed its doubts and feels like plain fact. Psychologists call the rising pull of a discounted message, once its source falls away, the sleeper effect.
. . .
There is a blunter cousin. Sheer repetition alone makes a claim feel true, even one you know better than to believe. That is the illusory truth effect, and Lisa Fazio’s work on it is in the optional reading; we will come back to it.
. . .
A scrolling feed runs both at once: content in, source gone, and the same lines again tomorrow.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
section: Where do the orphans come from?
text:
Where do the orphans come from?
Ask where forgotten-source beliefs actually start. Almost every one is forgotten testimony. Someone told you, or wrote it down; you kept the claim and lost the speaker.
. . .
So “may I trust a memory whose source I have lost” and “is testimony a way of knowing” are not two questions. Memory is where testimony goes to lose its source.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
Which sets up next time
You trust your forgotten-source memories constantly, and you have no choice about it. But once you do, it is hard to turn to a living speaker and demand they prove their reliability before you will believe a word.
That is the pressure point for next time, when we ask whether testimony stands on its own.

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
Reading
Required:

“Epistemological Problems of Memory,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §2.4 (Preservationism and Generativism).

Recommended:

Lisa K. Fazio et al., “Knowledge Does Not Protect Against Illusory Truth.”

title: Evidence and the Senses II: What Memory Keeps
text:
Loose end (optional)
Even deduction leans on this. Once a proof runs longer than you can hold in mind at once, you accept the conclusion because you remember checking each step, not because you are surveying the whole thing now.
Even the safest knowledge is not free of memory.

title: Why Trust Science, and How Trust Breaks
text:
You can judge experts without judging their work. Useful as that is, science is more than a heap of individual experts, and its authority does not rest on any one of them.



The usual story says science earns its trust by following the Method, a recipe that turns observation into truth. Naomi Oreskes argues there is no such recipe, and never was.
What science has instead is a process. A claim is handed to a community trained to attack it, and only what survives the attack is kept.



On this picture a result is trustworthy to the degree that it has met serious, varied criticism and held up.
The variety is doing real work. A group that shares one blind spot will miss the same things every time. A mixed group catches what any one member would let slide.



This is why a consensus carries weight. A vote among experts does not make a claim true. What a settled agreement shows is that the claim has run the gauntlet and is still standing.
The trap is manufactured controversy, a staged quarrel got up to make a closed question look open. Telling the real argument from the staged one is most of the work.

section: Two ways to be cut off
text:
Two ways to be cut off
C. Thi Nguyen pulls apart two things people often lump together. One is easy to fix. The other is not.

title: Why Trust Science, and How Trust Breaks
text:
The epistemic bubble
A bubble is a gap. You have simply not been exposed to the other side, because of whom you follow and what your feed puts in front of you.
Bubbles pop on contact. Let the missing voices in and the bubble is gone.

title: Why Trust Science, and How Trust Breaks
text:
The echo chamber
A chamber is the harder case. Inside one you have been brought to distrust the outside actively, so its experts arrive pre-labelled as liars.
Show a chamber the contrary evidence and it can grip harder, since the source was discredited for you in advance. Getting out tends to take a wholesale reset of whom you trust.

title: Why Trust Science, and How Trust Breaks
text:
What the chamber goes after
Notice its target. A chamber aims straight at Anderson’s signals.
It issues its own credentials, stages its own consensus, and teaches you to read honesty as betrayal. The very cues you use to place your trust are the ones it captures.

title: Why Trust Science, and How Trust Breaks
text:
The tour so far
We have followed knowledge from other people a long way: inference and its limits, testimony and whether it reduces, and trust scaled up to whole institutions.

title: Why Trust Science, and How Trust Breaks
text:
The source we never questioned
One thing has sat under all of it, taken on faith since the first day. Perception. We leaned on it as the bedrock and never asked what it actually hands us.
That is the next move, and it opens onto the mind.

C. Thi Nguyen, “Escape the Echo Chamber,” Aeon.

Recommended: Naomi Oreskes, “Defending science in a post-fact era” (Harvard Gazette, 2019), where she lays out her five pillars of trustworthy science.

title: What Utilitarianism Is
text:
Phil 101, Class 15. Read this before class. It is about 1,350 words.
About these extracts. Mill’s Utilitarianism appeared in 1863. Printed here are the first five pargraphs from the second chapter. Mill states his theory, and then responds to the objection that a theory built on pleasure is fit only for pigs. The chapter carries on for about another eight thousand words, answering further objections. You are not asked to read those, though you are welcome to.
The text comes from Project Gutenberg’s edition of Utilitarianism, eBook 11224, which reprints the seventh edition of 1879. The work is in the public domain, and the full text is at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11224.

The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness. By happiness is intended pleasure, and the absence of pain; by unhappiness, pain, and the privation of pleasure. To give a clear view of the moral standard set up by the theory, much more requires to be said; in particular, what things it includes in the ideas of pain and pleasure; and to what extent this is left an open question. But these supplementary explanations do not affect the theory of life on which this theory of morality is grounded—namely, that pleasure, and freedom from pain, are the only things desirable as ends; and that all desirable things (which are as numerous in the utilitarian as in any other scheme) are desirable either for the pleasure inherent in themselves, or as means to the promotion of pleasure and the prevention of pain.
Now, such a theory of life excites in many minds, and among them in some of the most estimable in feeling and purpose, inveterate dislike. To suppose that life has (as they express it) no higher end than pleasure—no better and nobler object of desire and pursuit—they designate as utterly mean and grovelling; as a doctrine worthy only of swine, to whom the followers of Epicurus were, at a very early period, contemptuously likened; and modern holders of the doctrine are occasionally made the subject of equally polite comparisons by its German, French, and English assailants.
When thus attacked, the Epicureans have always answered, that it is not they, but their accusers, who represent human nature in a degrading light; since the accusation supposes human beings to be capable of no pleasures except those of which swine are capable. If this supposition were true, the charge could not be gainsaid, but would then be no longer an imputation; for if the sources of pleasure were precisely the same to human beings and to swine, the rule of life which is good enough for the one would be good enough for the other. The comparison of the Epicurean life to that of beasts is felt as degrading, precisely because a beast’s pleasures do not satisfy a human being’s conceptions of happiness. Human beings have faculties more elevated than the animal appetites, and when once made conscious of them, do not regard anything as happiness which does not include their gratification. I do not, indeed, consider the Epicureans to have been by any means faultless in drawing out their scheme of consequences from the utilitarian principle. To do this in any sufficient manner, many Stoic, as well as Christian elements require to be included. But there is no known Epicurean theory of life which does not assign to the pleasures of the intellect; of the feelings and imagination, and of the moral sentiments, a much higher value as pleasures than to those of mere sensation. It must be admitted, however, that utilitarian writers in general have placed the superiority of mental over bodily pleasures chiefly in the greater permanency, safety, uncostliness, &c., of the former—that is, in their circumstantial advantages rather than in their intrinsic nature. And on all these points utilitarians have fully proved their case; but they might have taken the other, and, as it may be called, higher ground, with entire consistency. It is quite compatible with the principle of utility to recognise the fact, that some kinds of pleasure are more desirable and more valuable than others. It would be absurd that while, in estimating all other things, quality is considered as well as quantity, the estimation of pleasures should be supposed to depend on quantity alone.
If I am asked, what I mean by difference of quality in pleasures, or what makes one pleasure more valuable than another, merely as a pleasure, except its being greater in amount, there is but one possible answer. Of two pleasures, if there be one to which all or almost all who have experience of both give a decided preference, irrespective of any feeling of moral obligation to prefer it, that is the more desirable pleasure. If one of the two is, by those who are competently acquainted with both, placed so far above the other that they prefer it, even though knowing it to be attended with a greater amount of discontent, and would not resign it for any quantity of the other pleasure which their nature is capable of, we are justified in ascribing to the preferred enjoyment a superiority in quality, so far outweighing quantity as to render it, in comparison, of small account.
Now it is an unquestionable fact that those who are equally acquainted with, and equally capable of appreciating and enjoying, both, do give a most marked preference to the manner of existence which employs their higher faculties. Few human creatures would consent to be changed into any of the lower animals, for a promise of the fullest allowance of a beast’s pleasures; no intelligent human being would consent to be a fool, no instructed person would be an ignoramus, no person of feeling and conscience would be selfish and base, even though they should be persuaded that the fool, the dunce, or the rascal is better satisfied with his lot than they are with theirs. They would not resign what they possess more than he, for the most complete satisfaction of all the desires which they have in common with him. If they ever fancy they would, it is only in cases of unhappiness so extreme, that to escape from it they would exchange their lot for almost any other, however undesirable in their own eyes. A being of higher faculties requires more to make him happy, is capable probably of more acute suffering, and is certainly accessible to it at more points, than one of an inferior type; but in spite of these liabilities, he can never really wish to sink into what he feels to be a lower grade of existence. We may give what explanation we please of this unwillingness; we may attribute it to pride, a name which is given indiscriminately to some of the most and to some of the least estimable feelings of which mankind are capable; we may refer it to the love of liberty and personal independence, an appeal to which was with the Stoics one of the most effective means for the inculcation of it; to the love of power, or to the love of excitement, both of which do really enter into and contribute to it: but its most appropriate appellation is a sense of dignity, which all human beings possess in one form or other, and in some, though by no means in exact, proportion to their higher faculties, and which is so essential a part of the happiness of those in whom it is strong, that nothing which conflicts with it could be, otherwise than momentarily, an object of desire to them. Whoever supposes that this preference takes place at a sacrifice of happiness-that the superior being, in anything like equal circumstances, is not happier than the inferior-confounds the two very different ideas, of happiness, and content. It is indisputable that the being whose capacities of enjoyment are low, has the greatest chance of having them fully satisfied; and a highly-endowed being will always feel that any happiness which he can look for, as the world is constituted, is imperfect. But he can learn to bear its imperfections, if they are at all bearable; and they will not make him envy the being who is indeed unconscious of the imperfections, but only because he feels not at all the good which those imperfections qualify. It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. And if the fool, or the pig, is of a different opinion, it is because they only know their own side of the question. The other party to the comparison knows both sides.

title: Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion
text:
Phil 101, Class 26. Read this before class. It is about 1,050 words.
About these extracts. On Liberty appeared in 1859. Its second chapter is the case against silencing opinions, and it runs to about 16,700 words. Printed here are the two ends of it: the principle stated as strongly as it is ever stated, and the summary at the close of the chapter of the four grounds established for it. Before them is the dedication, which stands at the front of the book.
On the authorship. The book was published under John Stuart Mill’s name alone, and older editions print it that way. It is now commonly credited to Harriet Taylor Mill as well, and the Hackett edition of 2026 was the first to put both names on the title page. Mill says that they wrote it together in his Autobiography:

The Liberty was more directly and literally our joint production than anything else which bears my name, for there was not a sentence of it that was not several times gone through by us together, turned over in many ways, and carefully weeded of any faults, either in thought or expression, that we detected in it.

Note what he singles out: this book, as against everything else he wrote. There is support that does not rest on his word, in stylometric work by Christoph Schmidt-Petri, Michael Schefczyk and Lilly Osburg (Utilitas, 2022), arguing that the writing is not all in one hand.
You have spent a good part of this term on when to believe what you are told. Mill is a witness with an interest, writing in grief for his wife. The dedication below is his too, and it is doing several things at once. Read both with the distinction in mind.
On the text. The chapter comes from Project Gutenberg’s edition of On Liberty, eBook 34901, which names Mill alone. The work is in the public domain, and the full text is at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/34901. One footnote marker has been removed. The italic line between the two extracts is mine.


Dedication
To the beloved and deplored memory of her who was the inspirer, and in part the author, of all that is best in my writings—the friend and wife whose exalted sense of truth and right was my strongest incitement, and whose approbation was my chief reward—I dedicate this volume. Like all that I have written for many years, it belongs as much to her as to me; but the work as it stands has had, in a very insufficient degree, the inestimable advantage of her revision; some of the most important portions having been reserved for a more careful re-examination, which they are now never destined to receive. Were I but capable of interpreting to the world one-half the great thoughts and noble feelings which are buried in her grave, I should be the medium of a greater benefit to it than is ever likely to arise from anything that I can write, unprompted and unassisted by her all but unrivalled wisdom.



I. The principle
The time, it is to be hoped, is gone by, when any defence would be necessary of the “liberty of the press” as one of the securities against corrupt or tyrannical government. No argument, we may suppose, can now be needed, against permitting a legislature or an executive, not identified in interest with the people, to prescribe opinions to them, and determine what doctrines or what arguments they shall be allowed to hear. This aspect of the question, besides, has been so often and so triumphantly enforced by preceding writers, that it need not be specially insisted on in this place. Though the law of England, on the subject of the press, is as servile to this day as it was in the time of the Tudors, there is little danger of its being actually put in force against political discussion, except during some temporary panic, when fear of insurrection drives ministers and judges from their propriety; and, speaking generally, it is not, in constitutional countries, to be apprehended that the government, whether completely responsible to the people or not, will often attempt to control the expression of opinion, except when in doing so it makes itself the organ of the general intolerance of the public. Let us suppose, therefore, that the government is entirely at one with the people, and never thinks of exerting any power of coercion unless in agreement with what it conceives to be their voice. But I deny the right of the people to exercise such coercion, either by themselves or by their government. The power itself is illegitimate. The best government has no more title to it than the worst. It is as noxious, or more noxious, when exerted in accordance with public opinion, than when in or opposition to it. If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind. Were an opinion a personal possession of no value except to the owner; if to be obstructed in the enjoyment of it were simply a private injury, it would make some difference whether the injury was inflicted only on a few persons or on many. But the peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race; posterity as well as the existing generation; those who dissent from the opinion, still more than those who hold it. If the opinion is right, they are deprived of the opportunity of exchanging error for truth: if wrong, they lose, what is almost as great a benefit, the clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error.
It is necessary to consider separately these two hypotheses, each of which has a distinct branch of the argument corresponding to it. We can never be sure that the opinion we are endeavouring to stifle is a false opinion; and if we were sure, stifling it would be an evil still.
First: the opinion which it is attempted to suppress by authority may possibly be true. Those who desire to suppress it, of course deny its truth; but they are not infallible. They have no authority to decide the question for all mankind, and exclude every other person from the means of judging. To refuse a hearing to an opinion, because they are sure that it is false, is to assume that their certainty is the same thing as absolute certainty. All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility. Its condemnation may be allowed to rest on this common argument, not the worse for being common.

[Mill and Taylor Mill argue the first two grounds at length, over some fourteen thousand words. The chapter closes by drawing all four together.]



II. The four grounds
We have now recognised the necessity to the mental well-being of mankind (on which all their other well-being depends) of freedom of opinion, and freedom of the expression of opinion, on four distinct grounds; which we will now briefly recapitulate.
First, if any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true. To deny this is to assume our own infallibility.
Secondly, though the silenced opinion be an error, it may, and very commonly does, contain a portion of truth; and since the general or prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely or never the whole truth, it is only by the collision of adverse opinions, that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied.
Thirdly, even if the received opinion be not only true, but the whole truth; unless it is suffered to be, and actually is, vigorously and earnestly contested, it will, by most of those who receive it, be held in the manner of a prejudice, with little comprehension or feeling of its rational grounds. And not only this, but, fourthly, the meaning of the doctrine itself will be in danger of being lost, or enfeebled, and deprived of its vital effect on the character and conduct: the dogma becoming a mere formal profession, inefficacious for good, but cumbering the ground, and preventing the growth of any real and heartfelt conviction, from reason or personal experience.

title: PHIL 101: Introduction to Philosophy
text:
Key Points

This course is an introduction to philosophy through a set of connected questions: how we ought to reason, when a belief is rational, what minds and persons are, and what we owe each other.
No background is assumed. Most readings are short, and all of them are free.
The course meets twice a week for lecture and twice a week for discussion section. Attendance at both matters, and a good deal of the assessment happens in the room.
Assessment is spread across many small pieces rather than concentrated in a few large ones. Nothing worth more than 3% falls due before the sixth week.
There is one essay, worth 25%, and it comes at the end of a sequence designed to teach you how to write it.

title: PHIL 101: Introduction to Philosophy
text:
Course Description
Philosophy starts from questions that are easy to ask and hard to answer. This course takes a handful of them and works through what has been said in reply, from classical India and ancient Greece to work published in the last few years.
We begin with reasoning. What makes an argument a good one, what separates the inferences that are safe from the ones that pay, and why does a run of evidence never quite settle what comes next?
The second unit asks when a belief is rational. We’ll start with the question of when perceptual beliefs are rational, and then move onto other cases. A particular focus will be beliefs formed via testimony. This raises both theoretical questions, what makes a belief formed via testimony rational, and practical questions, in a world like this, who should we trust?
The middle of the course is about minds. The big question here is one of the oldest in philosophy: what is the relationship between minds and bodies. We’ll get to that by looking again at perception, and in particular thinking about the conscious aspects of perception, what it feels like to perceive the world the way we do.
The rest of the course is about value. What makes an action right, what makes a life go well, what makes you the same person you were at five, and what a state may and may not do to you. We end on free speech, which sends us back to where we started, since the case for free speech is a claim about how a group of people reasons its way to the truth.

text:
Submit Your Own Work
Anything you put your name to, and hand in, has to be your own work. Copying passages from a textbook, borrowing someone else’s work, paying someone to do it for you, or handing the assignment to a chatbot, are ways of creating documents that are not your own work, and are violations of academic integrity. Getting someone (or something) else to translate what you wrote is also not acceptable for this course.
In practice, we have the following two rules on everything written that you turn in.

There must be an acknowledgments section where you record all the help you got, from friends, family, books, computers, etc. You should overshare here; it’s fine to get lots of help, and as long as the result is your own work, we aren’t going to worry what help you got. One exception to this: if if you do use any online tools (that includes search engines, now that they have language models built it) you must keep records of everything you ask them. Do not use anyone else’s account, or any account you cannot access the history of, for any course-related purpose.
For anything you write, you have to be able to answer two questions: What did you mean by that? and Why did you write that?. That’s what we mean by something being your own work; you can explain and defend it.

NOTE FOR GSIs - THIS IS IMPORTANT AND WILL BE SOMETHING YOU HAVE TO DO; WE SHOULD TALK ABOUT THE LOGISTICS OF THIS AND WHETHER IT CAN BE IMPROVED
To that end, we will frequently audit the turned in work. In practice, that means we’ll ask the auditee (that might be you!) to explain, in person, what they meant by various claims, and why they wrote it. We will audit work that we think is suspicious, and we will also do some audits at random. If we audit you, this does not mean we think you cheated; it could be random. It’s annoying for us, and I’m sure annoying for you, that we have to do this, but the evidence is that people turning in work which is not their own is a bit out of control.

Class Schedule
Readings are listed under the class they are for, and should be done before that class. Where more than one required item is listed, do the shortest one first.
The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu) and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (iep.utm.edu) have entries on nearly every topic in this course. Both are free and written by specialists. Checking them is a good move whenever a reading or a lecture leaves you stuck, whether or not a particular entry is listed below. These entries are often long, and the listings below will sometimes point you to the part of an entry that’s most relevant.

Week 1: Getting Started

Tuesday, September 01 (Lecture 1) — Introduction
What the course is about, and how it works. No reading.


Thursday, September 03 (Lecture 2) — Deduction: the logic game
We play a deduction game in class. No reading.



Week 2: Risky Inference

Tuesday, September 08 (Lecture 3) — Induction, analogy, and explanation
Required: Arthur Conan Doyle, “The Boscombe Valley Mystery,” in The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Project Gutenberg). One passage only, about two pages: from “Sherlock Holmes was transformed when he was hot upon such a scent as this” to “There are several other indications, but these may be enough to aid us in our search.” This isn’t a philosophy paper, but we’ll start with the philosophical presuppositions behind it.
Recommended: The rest of the story.


Thursday, September 10 (Lecture 4) — Grue
Required: Jonathan Weisberg, “The Grue Paradox,” in Odds & Ends, appendix C.
Recommended: Sven Neth, “Goodman’s New Riddle of Induction Explained in Words of One Syllable.”



Week 3: When Is a Belief Rational?

Tuesday, September 15 (Lecture 5) — Perceptual evidence, and how many sources of knowledge there are
Required: Todd R. Long, “Epistemic Justification: What is Rational Belief?” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Required: Stephen Phillips and Anand Vaidya SEP, “Epistemology in Classical Indian Philosophy”, SEP, §1.1.
Recommended: Ted Poston, “Foundationalism”, IEP, §§1–2.


Thursday, September 17 (Lecture 6) — Memory and the forgotten source
Required: SEP, “Epistemological Problems of Memory,” §2.4.
Recommended: Lisa K. Fazio et al., “Knowledge Does Not Protect Against Illusory Truth.”



Week 4: Believing Other People

Tuesday, September 22 (Lecture 7) — Does testimony stand on its own?
Required: Dhirendra Mohan Datta, “Testimony as a Method of Knowledge,” Mind 36 (1927): 354–358.
Recommended: Dan Sperber et al., “Epistemic Vigilance,” Mind & Language 25 (2010).


Thursday, September 24 (Lecture 8) — Whom do you trust?
Required: Elizabeth Anderson, “Democracy, Public Policy, and Lay Assessments of Scientific Testimony,” Episteme (2011), §2 (pp. 145–149).
Recommended: SEP, “The Social Dimensions of Scientific Knowledge,” §2.



Week 5: Science, and the Mind

Tuesday, September 29 (Lecture 9) — Why trust science, and how trust breaks
Required: C. Thi Nguyen, “Escape the Echo Chamber” (Aeon).
Recommended: Naomi Oreskes, “Defending science in a post-fact era” (Harvard Gazette, 2019).
Module Quiz 1 (Lectures 1–9) opens after class, due Sunday. (NOTE FOR GSIs; should I just post the questions earlier?)


Thursday, October 01 (Lecture 10) — Perception reconsidered
Required: Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy, ch. 1, “Appearance and Reality.”
Recommended: SEP, “The Problem of Perception,” §2, “The Argument from Illusion”; and IEP, “Sense-Data”.



Week 6: Consciousness
Short Answer 1 is written in section this week.

Tuesday, October 06 (Lecture 11) — What it is like
Required: Thomas Nagel, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?”. Note this is slightly more reading than most days in class.


Thursday, October 08 (Lecture 12) — The hard problem, and Mary
Required: Tufan Kıymaz, “The Knowledge Argument Against Physicalism” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Required: Frank Jackson, “What Mary Didn’t Know”. It’s probably best to read Kıymaz first as background for Jackson’s paper.
Short Answer 2 goes out after class, on Lectures 10 to 12, due Friday 23 October.



Week 7: Dualism

Tuesday, October 13 (Lecture 13) — The case for
Required: Peter Adamson, “What can Avicenna teach us about the mind-body problem?” (Aeon Ideas).
Required: Marc Bobro, “René Descartes’ Meditations 4–6” (1000-Word Philosophy). The most important part is the end, on Meditation VI.
Recommended: Jacob Berger, “The Mind-Body Problem,” the “Varieties of Dualism” section; and Descartes, Meditation VI itself (Bennett, Early Modern Texts).


Thursday, October 15 (Lecture 14) — The case against
Required: Jacob Berger, “The Mind-Body Problem: What Are Minds?” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Recommended: IEP, “Identity Theory”, introduction; and Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia and Descartes, correspondence of 1643.
Module Quiz 2 (Lectures 10–14) opens after class, due Sunday 1 November.



Week 8: Consequentialism
Short Answer 2 due Friday, October 23.

Tuesday, October 20 — Fall Study Break, no class


Thursday, October 22 (Lecture 15) — Consequentialism
Required: Shane Gronholz, “Consequentialism and Utilitarianism” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Required: J. S. Mill, Utilitarianism ch. 2, first five paragraphs (extract posted to Canvas).
Recommended: SEP, “Consequentialism”, §1, “Classic Utilitarianism.”



Week 9: Deontology and Trolleys

Tuesday, October 27 (Lecture 16) — Deontology
Required: Andrew Chapman, “Deontology: Kantian Ethics” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Recommended: SEP, “Deontological Ethics,” §1, “Deontology’s Foil: Consequentialism”; and Immanuel Kant, Groundwork, Section I, especially the opening on the good will and the passages on universal law.


Thursday, October 29 (Lecture 17) — Trolley problems and objections
Required: Gabriel Andrade, “The Doctrine of Double Effect” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Required: Judith Jarvis Thomson, “The Trolley Problem”, sections I and II.



Week 10: What Makes a Life Go Well

Tuesday, November 03 (Lecture 18) — What is welfare?
Required: Richard Y. Chappell and Darius Meissner, “Theories of Well-Being”, the introduction.
Required: Roger Crisp, “Well-Being”, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §1, “The Concept.”


Thursday, November 05 (Lecture 19) — Hedonism
Required: SEP, “Well-Being”, §4.1, “Hedonism.”
Required: Robert Nozick, “The Experience Machine”. (This is just a two page excerpt.)
Short Answer 2 comes back Friday, with the essay question. (AGAIN, IT MIGHT BE BEST TO DISTRIBUTE ESSAY QUESTIONS EARLIER)



Week 11: Desire, and the Objective List

Tuesday, November 10 (Lecture 20) — Desire and preference theories
Required: SEP, “Well-Being,” §4.2, “Desire Theories.”
Recommended: “Theories of Well-Being” (utilitarianism.net), the desire-theory section.


Thursday, November 12 (Lecture 21) — Objective lists, and who has a welfare
Required: SEP, “Well-Being”, §4.3, “Objective List Theories.”
Required: “The Moral Status of Animals” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Recommended: “If AIs Can Feel Pain, What Is Our Responsibility Towards Them?” (Aeon).
Recommended: Walter Sinnott-Armstrong and Vincent Conitzer, “How Much Moral Status Could Artificial Intelligence Ever Achieve?”. If you are writing an essay on this topic, this is Required.
Module Quiz 3 (Lectures 15–21) opens after class.



Week 12: The Self

Tuesday, November 17 (Lecture 22) — Personal identity: the cases
Required: Kristin Seemuth Whaley, “Psychological Approaches to Personal Identity” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Required: Derek Parfit, “Divided Minds and the Nature of Persons”.
Recommended: Chad Vance, “Personal Identity: How We Exist Over Time” (1000-Word Philosophy).


Thursday, November 19 (Lecture 23) — What matters in survival
Required: John Locke, Essay, II.xxvii, §§9, 14, and 26.
Required: Daniel Weltman, “The Buddhist Theory of No-Self” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Required: Jessica Gordon-Roth, “Locke on Personal Identity”, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §1, “Locke on Persons and Personal Identity: The Basics.”
Recommended: Locke, II.xxvii, §§9–26 entire, for anyone who wants to see the details of Locke’s view in a more original form.



Week 13: Law
Essay due Monday, November 23.

Tuesday, November 24 (Lecture 24) — Why obey the law?
Required: John Protavi, “Plato’s Crito”. Read this first.
Required: Plato, Crito. (Jowett translation, Project Gutenberg)


Thursday, November 26 — Thanksgiving recess, no class



Week 14: Punishment and Speech

Tuesday, December 01 (Lecture 25) — Theories of punishment
Required: Travis Joseph Rodgers, “Theories of Punishment” (1000-Word Philosophy).
Recommended: SEP, “Legal Punishment”, the consequentialist and retributivist sections.


Thursday, December 03 (Lecture 26) — Free speech and the marketplace of ideas
Required: Mark Satta, “Free Speech” (1000-Word Philosophy)

Week 15: Ending

Module Quiz 4 (Lectures 22–27) opens after class, due Friday.

No reading. Bring questions.

The section component
We should decide what to do with the 20%. That’s a lot for you, but on the other hand, it gives you plenty of things to do in class, and two classes a week is a lot to prep. So I think we should go with something like

Short Answer 1 ~8%

But we can alter point 2, or add something else. I think it would probably be best to be uniform across the sections, but I’m willing to be talked out of it.


Consequences of the November essay deadline
The essay is due Monday 23 November so that marked essays go back before the examination.
Short Answer 2 is marked across two weeks, 23 October to 6 November. That’s an important deadline to hit, because the students should use the feedback from in in essay 1. Also, this should get more feedback than either short answer 1 or frankly the essay. (And definitely more than the exam.)
Then essay marking doesn’t have as hard a deadline; ideally 2 weeks after it’s turned in, but a bit of slippage here isn’t the end of the world.
The stuff at the end isn’t as crucial to the grading, because it only shows up on one quiz and an exam. That may result in some loss of enthusiasm. Now maybe that’s fine; it’s the end of term. And free speech normally gets enough enthusiasm anyway. And no matter what the grade, students over-index on the importance of the exam. But if you’re worried, we could move some of the 20% to in class activities after the essay is due in.
Short Answer 1 is meant to be in class, and this could cause accommodations complications. We should flag this early, and get on top of any issues. The same goes for any other in class writing assignments you want to do.
